The appellants, who were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff, filed a suit for a declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property in dispute. The suit was dismissed on the ground that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the suit property and, therefore, a suit for declaration and an order of injunction was not maintainable. The defendants, however, contended that the suit was barred by res judicata and that the suit had been barred by resjudicata. The Trial Court upheld the plaintiffs contention and dismissed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the suit filed by the appellants was barred by the principle of res judicata and, therefore the suit was not maintainable and deserved to be dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The suit was not barred by res Judicata. The suit had been filed in a competent court having jurisdiction at the date of its institution. It would appear unfair to the defendants, and would be for the Trial Court to determine the course of action to be adopted in the light of the guidelines indicated hereinabove. [1020B] 1.2 The plaintiff was not a tenant in respect of the suit land. He was not a trespasser in the property. He was liable to be evicted therefrom. He was, therefore, entitled to the possession of the property. His remedy would, therefore, be to approach the Mamlatdar for decision and after his decision is received by the Civil Court if the issue is held against him. [1021C D] 1.3 The suit was barred under section 58(2) of the Act. [1022D] 2. The suit filed by a person who is a deemed tenant under section 4 of the Act if evicted from the land on or after 1st July, 1962, his remedy under section 8(2) is to approach the authority under the Act for recovery of possession of the land of which he has been dispossessed. In such a situation the remedy may not be the one available in the case of a tenant other than a deemed tenant whose case is not governed by section 8(1) of the Rent Act. But in the case in hand, the suit was filed in a court having jurisdiction in the area in which the suit property was situated. The suit, therefore, was barred by limitation. [1023E F]

The appellant was the sole executor of the will alleged to have been executed by one Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, and died in December 1908. The appellant claimed a decree for possession against respondent 1. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant filed a suit for possession against the respondent. The trial Court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree. The appellant appealed to this Court. The High Court held that the will was not proved by the appellant, and that the will had been executed by her. The High court also held that the appellant was entitled to dispose of the properties under the will. The High. Court also held that it was not proved that the will executed by her was not proved. The High, Court also held in favour of the appellant. The appellant then appealed to this court. Held, that the High Court was not justified in recording its findings on two other issues in the present proceedings. The High Courts were not justified in holding that the will did not prove the will. It was not proved in the present case that the will in question was not proved, and that it was proved that the testator had signed the will. In the present case, the High Court had not properly considered all the relevant evidence. The High 'Court was not justified to record its findings on the two other issues. The HighCourt was not right in recording its finding on two other points. The High "Court " was not justified under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Power of Attorney was not a document of the nature referred to in the will. A will was not a will and was not proved to have been signed by the testator. The will was not in the nature of a will. The will did not show that the will bore the signature of the testatrix. The will had not been proved by the testator and the will had not proved that it was signed by the testatrix.

The appellant company, a company, was assessed to sales tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fall under entry No. 4 of the First Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the goods were not "electrical goods" falling within entry 41 of Schedule 1 of the Act. The High Court, however, held that the sales tax was not payable on the goods under entry No 4 of the Schedule 1 of that Act. The appellant company appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the entry under consideration links the taxable object with its general or ordinary use. The High court held that the appellant company was not "applied" to "goods" within entry 41. The High 'Court, however, did not accept this contention. The High, Court, however held that the words "not being such articles as are ordinarily used for other purposes" in entry No.4 of the Schedule I of the Act were not "agricultural machinery" within the meaning of entry No.14 of the Act, and that the appellant was not "agricultural" within the definition of "agricultural machinery". The High Court also held that the expression "other" in entry 4 of the Act was not "industrial machinery" within entry No. 14 of the Act and that the words 'not being such things as are ordinarily also used for other purpose than as "industrial machinery". The appellant company preferred appeals to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, the Court, HELD: The expression "other", in entry No 4 occurs in a schedule in which descriptions of goods to be taxed indicate that the expression 'required for use there with ' has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. The entry is not "industrial" within the Act. [566 B C] The expression "industrial machinery", is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. The entry does not include parts thereof. The entry refers to parts thereof. It is not necessary that the goods are not "agricultural". The entry is a residuary entry. The entry relates to "industrial machinery"; and the entry is a general entry. The word "industrial" is used in both the entries in the schedule. The word 'industrial ' is used in various entries, such as entry No. 3, and the word "industrial", is used for the purpose of the entry itself. The entry, therefore, refers to "industrial goods" and not "industrial goods". [566 C D]

The petitioners challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of the (67 of 1957) amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners contended that the notification was ultra vires the State Legislature and that the notification issued by it was ultra vires. The petitioners also contended that the State Government had no power to issue a notification under section 15 of 1957 and that the State was not bound to issue the notification under section 9 of the Act. The State Government contended that the power to issue the said notification was not delegated to the State Government and that the power was not delegated. The State of Gujarat, on the other hand, contended that the impugned notification was ultra virus and that the impugned notifications were ultra vires the provisions of the Act and that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the notification. The State contended that the Act was ultra vires and that the Act did not violate article 301 of the Constitution. The petitioners further contended that the provisions of section 9 of Gujarat Minor Mineral Concession Rules 1966 were ultra vires and the State Government was not bound by the provisions of that Act. The petitioners submitted that the impugned Notification was ultra vires as it was not a law made by the State Legislature. The petitioners, therefore, prayed for a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to issue a mandamus to the State to issue a Notification under section 15(1) of the Act amending the Gujarat Mineral Rules 1965. The State Legislature passed the Gujarat Minor Minerals Rules 1966 which was published in the Gazette on June 26. The petitioners challenged the vires of the Act on the ground that the Act had been enacted with a view to provide for the regulation of mines and development of minerals under the control of the Union and it was not open to the State Legislature to issue the same. The petitioners urged that the impugned Act was ultra viro the Constitution and that the provisions in the Act were ultra vires. Dismissing the petitions, the Court, HELD: 1. The impugned Act is ultra vires the Constitution. [416D] 1. The Act is not a law enacted by the Parliament and the State Legislature is competent to enact it. The Act has made provision with regard to the issue of prospecting licences and mining leases in respect of various kinds of minerals other than minor minerals and the procedure to be followed in the matter of issue of prospecting licence and mining leases. [416E] 2. The impugned notification was not ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature under article 246 of the Constitution and the State Act was not ultra virus. [416F] 3. The impugned notifications were not ultra vires. [416G] 4. The impugned Notification was not ultra law. The State legislature was competent to enact the impugned Act. The impugned Notifications were ultra vires as they were not made under the provisions of any law. [416H] 5. The impugned provisions of the impugned notifications are ultra vires the power of the State legislature. The impugned orders are ultra vires. They are not ultra vires of the Constitution, and are therefore, liable to be quashed. [416C]

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Brahmins of Manjakollai village in the year 1957. The appellant was elected to the office of a trustee by a member of the Sengunta community. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the trusteeship of the appellant was not hereditary. The High Court held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The appellant contended that the succession was not hereditary and that the right to the office was not hereditary in the sense that on the death of an existing mahant, his chela does not succeed to the office as a matter of course, because the successor acquires a right only by appointment and the authority to appoint is vested in the assembly of the bairagis and the worshippets. Held, that the appellant is a hereditary trustee within the meaning of the section. The right to the post of trustee in the present case was not hereditary within the meaning Of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The appellant 's right to the appointment of the trustee in the instant case was not a hereditary right. The right of the appellant to the office in question was not hereditary, because the office of the appellant being hereditary, the suit was for a fixed period of one year and not for life. The appellant had a right only 'by appointment and the authorities were right in holding that the office of trustee in a hereditary office was not a post abolished. The appellant could not succeed to his office as a hereditary trustee. The appellant is not a hereditary trustee of the office of Mahant. The appellant cannot succeed to his own office. The appellant, therefore, was not a Mahant within the meaning. The appellant must be deemed to be a hereditary trustee for the purpose of section 6(1) of the Act. The appellant has a right to the hereditary office and the authority of the trustee to appoint is not vested in the Sardar Mahant. The right is not a right to property. The right by which one set of men may, by succeeding another set, acquire a property in all the goods, movables and other chattels of a corporation. The fact of the transmission of the rights, estate, obligations and charges of a deceased person to his heir or heirs. " The appellant was not a trustee of the property of the appellant. The appellant did not acquire a right to a hereditary office. The right was not hereditary but was a hereditary right and the right to a permanent office was not heritable. The right, therefore, could not be said to be hereditary. The appellant can succeed to his place of residence. The right in the present ease was not hereditary because the office was abolished and the right of the Mahant to the office had been transferred to the appellant.

The appellant was convicted under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year in each case. The High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three appeals for offences under section 52 Of the Indian Post Offices Act, 1897. The appellant 's appeal to this Court was restricted to the acquittal of the appellant in respect of offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. Held, that the prosecution had failed to prove that the letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant and that the almirah was in the exclusive use of the appellant. The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 52 Of The Indian Post Office (Act, 1898) and the prosecution was not entitled under section 52 to the benefit. The appellant had not been convicted of the offence of theft. The appellant could not be convicted of the offences under section 53 Of the Indian Penal Act. The appellant must be deemed to be in exclusive possession of these articles and not merely in his joint possession along with his father because he had the key with him. The almirah was not in the exclusive occupation of the appellant, and the appellant could not have been convicted of any offence under section 52. The appellant, therefore, could not be held to be in possession of the keys of the almirah which was in his exclusive possession. The appellant did not, therefore, be held to have been in exclusive possession and was not entitled, to the benefit under section 52, Of the Indian Posts Office Act, 1908.

The partition of the suit property was not a result of any partition. The plaintiff, therefore, was not entitled for a decree for possession of the suit house. [735 D] 3. The plaintiff is not entitled to any share in the suit house as she had a 1 1/4 share in the partition. The share to which she had been living in the joint Family property was not in the joint possession of the plaintiff. [736 D] 4. Held, that the procedure under section 5 of the Act was substantially prejudicial to the assessee and the procedure prescribed in section 5(2) of the impugned Act was not violative of article 14. The procedure prescribed in sections 6, 7 and 8 of the Act in sections 5, 6 and7 of the Act, in so far as affects the persons proceeded against under that section being a piece of discriminatory legislation, infringed the fundamental rights of the petitioner. The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, New Delhi, was registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Federation was a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act. The Federation filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Federation 's order dated February 8, 1967, and the High Court held that the Federation was a 'commercial establishment ' within the meaning Of section 2(7) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. The High Court held the Federation was not a "commercial establishments" within the definition of "commercial establishment". The Federation appealed to this Court. HELD: The Federation was not an "commercial establishment", within the meaning ofs.2(5) Of the Act. [357 B] The Federation was an "commercial organisation" within the Act. It was not a 'commercial activity ' because by the Memorandum of Association, the Federation was established for a "commercial purpose" within the ambit of section 2 (5) of Delhi Shops and Establishment Act, 1956. The Federation had no business or trade in its business. The Federation could not, therefore, be a "commercial activity" within the purview of section 2 of the Act, and the Federation could not be a "industrial establishment" within section 2(27) of the Indian Act. [359 C D] The Federation had a secretary, and the members of the Federation were not members of the association. The Federation did not carry on any business carried on by the Federation. (5) Of Delhi Shops and establishments Act, 1957. The Federation cannot be a " commercial establishment" within Section 2(27). The Federation cannot, therefore, fall within the definition 'commercial establishment ', because by the memorandum of Association, it was established for the objects of preparing and publishing under gratuitous professional control, reports of judicial decisions, of issuing digests and other publications relating to legal subjects. [352 C D] R. K. Mittals case, (supra) referred to.

Held, that the order passed by the High Court was a colourable exercise and was not in the public interest. The appellant could not rest its case merely on r. 18 (a) and say that having acted under that rule there was nothing more to be said and that the industrial court cannot inquire into the causes that led to the termination of service under r. 18. The appellant cannot rest its case on the ground that the important witnesses, namely, the Engineer, the Secretary and other members of the staff, who were examined by the respondent, were taken by the appellant to the effect that the exercise was colourable and was not bona fide. The Tribunal had not considered the question whether it should be fixed on the basis of the age of the employees of the respondent company or whether it should have fixed the retirement age at 60. It was not correct to say that the age had to be raised to 58 and that it was open to the Tribunal to consider the question whether the age of compulsory retirement should be fixed in the light of the decision of this Court in the case of the Bombay region. The Tribunal was right. The Tribunal has not considered the evidence on record and has come to the conclusion that the age has to be raised at 55. The Tribunal 's conclusion that the retirement of the respondent workmen should be raised before the Tribunal was correct. The Tribunal, therefore, was right in taking the view that the age at 55 should be raised and that the retirement should be made on the basis that the age is raised to 60. The fact that in the Bombay region at least there is a general agree ment that the age will be raised to 55 and that in the present case the age of retire should be raised. The Tribunal therefore had to consider the matter afresh and decide the question whether in the circumstances of the case the age should not be raised to the age of 60.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fine. The High Court and the Court below were of the opinion that the appellants were themselves the dacoits, and convicted them under section 395. The High court and the Court were of the view that the presumption under section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act was not drawn from the circumstances of the case and that the presumption that they were dacoits was not drawn when the circumstances were proved. The High. Court and the courts below were of opinion that the presumption was not drawn on the circumstances of each case. The High 'Court and the Court found that the appellants had been convicted under section 396 of the Indian IPC and sentenced them to 5 years ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 100/ . The High Court also held that the appellants could not be convicted under section 397 of the Indian Code. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) The presumption that they are dacoits was only a presumption which could be drawn from the proved circumstances of the particular case. The presumption that the accused was involved in the crime was not drawn by the prosecution and the evidence on which the presumption could be drawn was not drawn in the case. The appellants were not convicted under section 412 of the Indian , and were therefore not liable to be convicted under that section. [723 F G] (ii) The presumption under section 113 of the Evidence Act was drawn from the facts of the case. [724 F] (iii) The presumption was not discharged by the prosecution. The presumption under the section was drawn from those facts. The presumption was drawn from circumstances which the one presumption or the other may be drawn. The presumption could be rebutted only by the evidence of the witnesses who were the dacoits. The presumption is stronger when the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is committed. The reasons are obvious. Disposal of the fruits, of crime requires the finding of a person ready to receive them and the shortness of time the nature of the property which is disposed of, that is to say, its quantity and its character determined whether the person who had the goods in his possession received them from another or was himself the thief or the dacoit. [725 F G]

The petitioners challenged the validity of Section 5 of the (12 of 1919) (Act No. XIV of 1919), by a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the impugned provisions of the Act were violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution and that the impugned provision was violative of the right guaranteed under Article 19(i)(g) and (2) of the constitution. The petitioners also contended that the Act was a Central enactment and that the Act did not violate the fundamental rights of the petitioners. The petitioners further contended that the provisions of the impugned Act were violative and that the provisions were violative of Article 19(6) of the (7) of the Constitutional. The petitioners, therefore, prayed for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to declare the impugned provisions as unconstitutional and to declare the provisions of section 5 of the Act as unconstitutional and void. The respondents contended that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the Act and that the petitioners had not challenged the vires of the Act. The respondents also contended that they had not placed any matter before the authorities under the Act and the High Court was not justified in holding that the impugned Act was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the Act was not a Central enactment but a State enactment. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned provisions are violative of the constitutional rights guaranteed by the Constitution and are, therefore, violative of the rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution, and are, accordingly, struck down. [223E] 2. The impugned Act is not violative of the equality clause of the Constitution because it is a State enactment and is not a State enactment, and the impugned Act is a State legislation. [223F] 3. The impugned provision is not violative or arbitrary. It is not necessary that the impugned statute is a State Act. [223G] 4. The impugned statute is not a Central Act but a State Act, and the State Act is a Central Act. The State Act is not a Union Act. The impugned legislation is not a law made by the State Legislature. The impugned enactment is not a legislation within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution as it is a Central enactment. [223B]

The appellants were carrying on business in drugs, chemicals, mercury, camphor and silk yam and as money lenders. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim of the appellants for deduction of the amount of interest on the amount of loan advanced by them. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the amount of Rs. 2,68,385/ and disallowed the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on appeal, held that the debt did not arise in the course of the appellants ' business as chemists and druggists nor in the course or of their money lending business. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that there was no debt due from the appellants and that the amount was not a debt due from them. The Tribunal also held that the amount of the loan advanced by the appellants to the Bombay firm was not a loan advanced to the Bombay company and that the interest on the loan was not a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(15) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court, in reference, held that in the circumstances of the case the amount was a debt due to the appellants and the interest on it was not a revenue receipt. The High court, however, took the view that the amount could not be deducted in the computation of the amount. The High 'Court, however, in appeal, held in favour of the Revenue. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The amounts in question were not a debt owed by the appellants. The interest on the loans was not a sum which could be deducted in computing the income of the assessee. [434 B] (ii) The amounts were not a loan made in the ordinary course of the money lending business of the assessee and were not loans made in the normal course of the business. [435 C] (iii) The amounts could not be said to be a debt due by the assessee. The interest was not a money lending business and the interest was not money lending business within the meaning Of section 2(14) of the Act. [436 D]

The appellant bank was a bank employee in banks which were not governed by the provisions of the Sastry Award. The appellant bank contended that the respondents made applications under section 33 C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for determination and computation of the benefit to which they were entitled under the Desai award as they were not satisfied with the fixation of their pay by the appellant bank under para 5.356 of the Desai award. The Desai award provided that the workmen would be fitted in the new scales of pay from January 1, 1962 on stage to stage adjustment basis. The Desai Award provided that the employees would first be fitted in new scales of Pay. The Desai Tribunal held that the respondents were entitled to the benefit of the Desai Award as they were drawing basic pay on January 1, 1959, and that the respondents would be fitted into the new scales on January 1. 1962. The Desai tribunal held that the appellant bank was entitled to the benefits of the Desai ' Award as they had been drawing basic pay at a particular stage in the time scale of the Sastri Award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal Decision (Bank Disputes) Decision (Bank Dispute) Decision ( Bank Disputes) Decision, 1970, and held that the employees were entitled to get the benefit of para 5.34 of the Desai Tribunal 's decision. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Desai award provides that the employees will be fitted in a new scale of pay from the beginning of the date of the award and will be entitled to the same pay as the employees of the other banks. [907 B] (2) The Desai Award provides that the workmen will be fitted into new scales of salary from January 1. 1959, the date of their appointment and will be fitted to the new scales. The bank actually fixed them at Rs. 176 on its own interpretation of the award. The bank thus fixed them at the same level as the employees in the Sastry award. The Bank then maintained the scale of pay of the employees in their new scales of emoluments. The Bank therefore, was entitled to get their basic pay on the basis of the new scales applicable to the Sastry. [908 B C] (3) The Desai 's contention that the Desai Award was not applicable to the appellant bank is not correct. The Desai ' case is that the Desai award provided for the fixation of the pay of the appellant bank on January 1 1962. This was the view of the Desai Court that the appellant Bank was entitled to two increments under para 5 of the Desai formula. The Desai formula was the same as the appellant 's pay was fixed at Rs. 182. The Bank was therefore entitled to the appellant Bank 's pay as on January 1 1959. [909 B C]

The appellants, who were the owners of the land, filed a suit for the recovery of their land. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The first appellant contended that the suit was not maintainable as the land was not the land but a lease by the Government as a policy decision to run a Five Star Hotel. The first respondent contended that the lease was a lease by Government and that the lease had been granted to the appellants. The trial court decreed the suit. The first appellate court held that the lease granted to the first appellant was a lease and that the first appellant had no right to the land. The first appeal was dismissed. The High Court, in appeal, held that the first respondent was not a tenant of the land but was a lessee under the Government. The High court, therefore, held that it was not a lease by a Government. The first Appellate Court, however, held that there was no lease by the government and that the appellants were not entitled to the benefit of the lease. The High 'Court, therefore, allowed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the lease in question was a lease for a period of five years and that the second respondent was not entitled to claim the benefit of lease. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The first appellant who is a trade union ist had not espoused any grievance of the mazdoors before the High Court. It was only when courts are apprised of gross violation of fundamental rights by a group or a class action or when basic human rights are invaded or when there are complaints of such acts as shock the judicial conscience that the courts, particularly, the courts, especially the courts, would leave aside procedural shackles and hear such petitions and extend its jurisdiction under all available provisions for remedying the hardships and miseries of the needy, the under dog and the neglected. [240D E] 1.2 The first appellant, who is a Trade Union, has not espoused a grievance of the lurking out of the land. He is a trade Union. The first petitioner does not represent all the mazdoors. He is not a tenant under the Government and is not a lessee under Government. The second petitioner does not have a case, again, sale of a Government property. Therefore, public auction has necessarily to be ruled out. Only on the basis of the lease, the first appellant who was a trade union, has not been a tenant under Government. [240E F] 1.3 The first appellant is a trade association. The first and the second appellant are the owners of land. The lease was the culmination after a long, elaborate and open procedure with nothing to hide which would be subject to ad verse criticism. It is only when courts were apprised of gross violations of fundamental rights, that the courts were apprised that the lease is a lease by itself. The first plaintiff does not represent the mazbour in the suit. It is not a lease for the land. It is a lease for an indefinite period. The first defendant does not represent a tenant under a Government

The appellant was detained under the impugned order of detention on the 8th June 1955, and was in detention for more than three years. The grounds of detention were vague. The grounds were vague and the grounds of detention mentioned only the grounds of non disclosure. The grounds did not indicate the grounds of the detention. The appellant was arrested on the 9th June 1954, and was detained under section 3 of the . The grounds of his detention were vague and did not indicate any grounds of detention. The grounds showed that the grounds of his arrest were vague and that the grounds were vague. Held, that the grounds did not disclose the grounds of grounds of detention and the grounds did no show that the grounds for non disclosure were vague. It was not necessary for the detaining authority to apply its mind to the existence or otherwise of the grounds of deten tion. The grounds could not be said to have prejudiced the detenu in any way. The grounds for non compliance with the grounds of preventive detention were vague, and the grounds were not vague. The order of detention was mala fide. The last two had been urged before the detaining authority and the grounds showed that there was no ground for non disclosure. Held, further, that the order of detention did not disclose any ground of detention. It was a case of mere non disclosure of facts which were not communicated to the detenue at the time of the detention, and the order of non disclosure was not mala fide. It was open to the detenu to make a representation to the detaining authority against the order of preventive detention. The order was mala fide and the grounds could not therefore be said to be vague. The fact that the detenue was furnished information, at the time when the grounds were furnished, was not sufficient to justify the non disclosure.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. He was removed from service by the Central Government under r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. The Central Government directed removal from service of the respondent. The Central Govt. ordered removal from service. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that the respondent was not a member of the Army Staff Service and was not a person subject to the Army Act. The Central Govern ment was directed to remove him from service. He was also directed to submit his explanation by way of defence. The Central government found him guilty of misconduct and passed an order removing him from service under r.14 of the Army rules, 1954, and the Central Government confirmed him. The Central Governor passed an order on April 9, 1959, removing him from the service. The Central Administrative Tribunal, which heard the petition, held that the respondent had not been a member of Army Staff Service, and that the order of the Central Government was not ultra vires the . The High Court, however, held that r. 14 was ultra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19(1) of the Act are "subject to" and the Central Govt. has thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions of section 45. [484 B C] (ii) The words 'subject to the Act ' occurring in section 2(a) of the Army Act are " subject to the provisions Of this Act" and the words "subject" occurring in s.19(1) are "subject" to the provisions o. the Act. The words " subject to this Act" are "subject, to the provisions, of this Act". The words "except the provisions of the Act" are not "subject to this Act". [484 C D] (iii) The words and expressions used in the Act are not " subject to any Act". The word "subject" is "subject to any Act" and not the words " subject" occurring in the Act. [485 C] (iv) The words" subject to the Act" occurring therein are "subject only to the provisions contained in the Act". [487 E]

The appellant was a Panchayat under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1946. The resolution was passed by the Panchayat with a view to levy octroi on the goods brought within its local area. The appellant was deemed under the Bombay General Clauses Act to be a public servant. On July 25, 1961 the Panchayat passed resolution No. 2 with a view that the octroi duty shall be imposed on the goods bringing within its local areas, the committee accepted the same. The conciliation Proceedings were held on January 19, 1952 and the conciliation proceeding was completed on January 17 and the proceedings went on till June 2, 1952. The conciliation commenced on January 17 between the appellant No 1 and its workmen on January 17 after the expiry of the period of 14 days. The conciliation authorities took the view that the conciliation proceedings could not be said to be pending when the report was received by them. The conciliation officers took the view, that the conciliation proceeding could not be deemed to have concluded in the case of the respondent. Held, that the Conciliation officer was not a judicial officer within the meaning of section 31(2) and the conciliation officer was not competent to proceed with that proceeding. The appellant was granted a licence to sell the said gold to the respondent. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968. The High Court held that section 28 of Gold Control Act was not applicable to the case. The High court held that section 27(6) of the Gold Act was not attracted to the case because the section did not provide any guidelines for the purpose of granting or renewing a license to a dealer. The High 'Court also held that section 29 of the Gold (Control) Act, 1966 was not applicable. The High. Court also held that the section did provide that the section confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator to grant or renew a license to any dealer. The appellant 's appeal to this Court was dismissed by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that section 28 was not applicable in the present case. The section does not provide any guideline for the purpose. The section merely provides that the Administrator may grant or renew any license to a person for the purpose specified therein. The section only provides that the Government may grant or renewal of a license to an applicant for the purpose mentioned therein. The power conferred on the Administrator is not absolute in as much as the Administrator can authorise the third person to carry on the business in the licensed premises of the dealer and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy and purposes of the Act and by the prime consideration that circumvention of the other provisions of the Act shall not be premitted. [958 B C] The object of the Act is to provide for the purpose for which the licence is granted. The object of granting or renew a licence to a dealer is to enable the Administrator to carry on his business as a dealer but the word 'region ' is not used in the Act. The object is to enable a person to carry out the business in a licensed premises to carry on business as a licensee but the word "region" is not used as a guide to the purpose of the Act. The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple, were appointed as trustees of the said properties by respondent No. 4. The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for possession of the properties in suit and a permanent injunction restraining respondents 1 to 3 from interfering with their possession. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the respondents were entitled to the possession of the said property. The High court held that the appellants were entitled to possession of the property and that the respondents had been removed from the management of the temple by respondent No 4. The High 'Court further held that the transfer of the properties to the respondents was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and that the transfer was not in contravention of the provisions of section 87 of the Act. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the transfer in question was not in compliance with the provisions Of section 87 of Act. The transfer was not a valid transfer and the transfer was in contravention of section 87. (ii) The transfer was in violation of section 87 and the transfer could not be said to be in contravention of any of the provisions Of the Act. (iii) The transfer in question did not amount to a transfer within the meaning of section 87, and the transfer did not amount in any way to a transfer. (iv) The transfer did not create any right in the properties. The transfer did no amount to a gift. The transfer could not therefore be said to have been made in contravention of a provision of the Act, and the transfers were not in contravention thereof. (v) The transfer amounted to a transfer and was not in violation of the provisions. (vi) The transfer could be said to amount to a sale within the meaning Of section 87. The transfer amounted in contravention of article 134 B of the Constitution. (vii) The transfer of the property in suit was not in the nature of a transfer within section 87. It was not in breach of section 87 but was in contravention thereof and the transfer amounted to an offence under section 135 of the Act which was made punishable under section 135. (viii) The transfer being in contravention of sections 87 and 135 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, the transfer was void. (ix) The transfer, in fact, was in contravention Of section 87 and was not therefore void. (x) The transfer constituted an offence under the Act.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was running a cinema hall in the city of Jammu in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. Held, that the respondent was acting within his authority in issuing the notice in question under section 12 of the , and the notice in terms did not confer any authority on him to go back upon his own contracts. The respondent cannot be said to act within his powers as Custodian of evacuee property. The provisions of section 12 do not by implication repeal statutes confer rights on lessees, and cannot be reconciled with the contention of the appellants that it confers no authority on him.

The appellants were convicted and each was sentenced to death under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court acquitted them of the offence under section 302 but convicted them under section 302. The High court convicted them under sections 302 and sentenced them to death. The High ' Court convicted them under the section and sentenced them. The High. Court convicted them. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the sentence of death was not a sentence of imprisonment for life. The High Courts were not justified in holding that section 377 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not applicable to the case. The fact that the High Courts had not given any special reasons for reducing the sentences of death in the case of Bhilia and Tukia, did not affect the question of sentence in the case. Held, further, that the facts disclosed did not warrant an inference of common intention. The facts disclosed did no warrant an inference that the appellants were guilty of murder. The facts in the present case showed that the appellants had been convicted under section 302 and sentenced to death. There was no reason to depart from the practice in this case. The appellants were convicted under section 326 of the Indian Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life and were sentenced to death for the offence under the section. The High, Court was right, in holding that there was no evidence to show that the appellants inflicted the fatal blows on the head with an axe which penetrates half an inch into the head. The High "Court was not justified in interfering with the sentence of imprisonment of life. The fact of the appellants having been convicted under sections 302, and sentenced to life imprisonment was not a sufficient ground for the High Court to interfere with the sentence. The fact, however, that the appellants did not appeal to the High Court, did not make any difference. The fact was that the appellants gave blows with an axe and that they had not received any injury. The fact did not affect their conviction under section 326. The fact however that they were convicted under sections 326 and sentenced to transportation for life was not a ground for the appeal to the Supreme Court.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on an ad hoc basis. He was confirmed in the post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an adhoc basis. The appellants, who were the trustees of the Math, filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math and that the Amauli properties were owned by the Math and the deity was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The High Court held that the A.mauli properties had been purchased by the Mahant and the Amaul was in possession of the properties. The High court held that the appellants were not entitled to the exemption under the will. The High 'Court, however, held that the trust properties were owned and possessed by the Math. The High. Court, however, did not agree with the High Court that the trust was a public trust. The High, Court, however held that the income from the properties in question was not derived from the properties of the Math and was not derived therefrom. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the A,mauli properties could not be said to belong to the Math or the deity. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The income from the property in question was derived from the property of the Math. It was not the property of a Math or the idol. The income from such property was derived from it. The income derived from the trust was derived from its properties. The income was derived from property of the temple and not from the property. The income of the property was derived by the Math from the property and not from its personal property. The property was not the personal property of the Mahant. The income could not be derived from the income derived from his property. The trust properties were described by the Mahant as properties of the temple. The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of the village panchayats in 1949 and the land allotted to them in substitution of the lands at evacuees was given quasi permanent allotment in another village. The appellants filed a revision application before the Custodian General, Evacuee Property, but the Additional Custodian for the State of Punjab cancelled the allotment of the lands in favour of the appellants. The Additional Custodian, however, dismissed the revision application on the ground that the appellants were not entitled to allotment of suburban land. The appellants preferred an appeal to the Custodian General. The Custodian General, however, allowed the appeal on the ground of delay and cancelled the allotment. The appellants appealed to the Custodian, who dismissed the appeal on merits. The Custodian, however dismissed the revision on the ground, inter alia, that the appellants had no locus standi to file the revision application. The appellants then filed a revision petition before the Custodian, which was dismissed. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the Custodian General was right in holding that the appellants could not make out a new case at this stage of argument. The appellants were not precluded from challenging the order of cancellation of the allotment in their favour by the Custodian General on the ground inter alia that the order of the Custodian was not a transfer of the property of the appellants to the manager and therefore could not be said to be an order of cancellation. The order of the Additional Custodian was not an order of the Deputy Custodian. The order was not a mere order of cancellation but was a mere order by the Custodian. The Custodian was not competent to cancel the allotment in favour of any one else. The order did not amount to a transfer of property of the appellant to the manager. The order could not be challenged on the ground only that it was an order of transfer of property. The order, however, did not amount either to a transfer or to a transfer. The order merely stated that the order was to be made by the Custodian and not to a transfer and it was not a case of cancellation of an allotment. The order does not amount to an order of a transfer of land. The order is not a mere an order of allotment but a mere order for the purpose of making an order of confirmation. The order must be a mere order or an order of an allotment and not a mere one. The order in the present case was not a sale of land but a transfer of a property in the compensation pool. The order made by the Additional Custodian on the ground merely stated that he was not a party to the proceedings before the Custodian. Held, further, that the order did not create any right in the appellants to make the allotment of land. Held, also, that the orders of the Additional Director of Evacuee Property, Evacuee Property and the Additional Custodian were not final and could not be questioned in the proceedings before him. The order passed by the Additional Director was not a final order of the evacuee property and was not a nullity.

The property in question was leased to the appellant under two lease deeds in favour of M/s India Automobiles. The first lease was dated 22.9.1947 and related to Door No. 2 (Item No. 1 in Schedule A to the plaint) covered an area of 4 grounds and 1515 sq. It belonged to several co owners. The rent was Rs. 150 per month. On 30.7.1953, the LIC moved two applications (being HRC Nos. 3310 and 3311 of 1965) in the court of the Rent Controller for fixation of a "fair rent" for each of the premises. The Rent Controller, on the basis of the rent fixed under the lease deed, held that the lease was a statutory lease and that the superstructure had been built by them. The appellant filed objections to the application. The Rent Control Tribunal held that the rent was payable by the appellant and that the building was let out to the respondent. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Rent Control Tribunal. The Tribunal held that there was a relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties and that the lease deed was a statutory tenancy and that the appellant was entitled to relief under the Madras Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950. The High Court, in appeal, held that there were two different tenancies and that the question of the relationship of landlord & tenant was one of fact and that the respondent was entitled to the relief of eviction under the Madras Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to decide the question of title and that the Rent Control Act did not provide for a machinery for recovery of the amount. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that there was no relationship of landlord, tenant and tenant between both the parties. [557E] The Rent Control Act does not provide for any machinery for recovery by the landlord of rent from the tenant. The Rent Act does not contemplate any machinery for the recovery of the rent from the landlord. The Rent controller has to deal with the matter in a fair and just manner. The Rent control Act does not make a distinction between a landlord and tenant and the Rent Controller has to deal in a fair manner. The Act does not envisage any machinery for recovering the rent from a tenant. The Act contemplates a machinery for the eviction of a tenant from the tenant and the tenant is entitled to recover the rent from him.
